title: Modeling
body:
[[Use Case Diagrams]]

The third step of [[Software Requirements Analysis]]: after you have recognised the problem
and evaluated the alternatives, you draw it. A model is a deliberately incomplete picture of
the system, and the incompleteness is the feature: it shows one aspect (who uses it, what
data flows, what states it has) with everything else stripped out, so it can be checked by a
person rather than compiled.

Two things a model buys you:

- **It is cheap to be wrong in.** Changing a diagram costs minutes; changing the
  implementation it would have produced costs weeks. This is the [[SDLC]] cost curve again.
- **It is readable by people who cannot read code.** [[Use Case Diagrams]] exist almost
  entirely for this reason, which is why they land late in analysis, when there is something
  to show the stakeholder.

Modelling continues past analysis into design, where [[OOM]] is the object-oriented version:
the same activity, applied to classes and their relationships rather than to the problem
domain.

Do not confuse this note with [[Models]], which means *process* models ([[Waterfall]],
[[Agile]]). Same root word, different thing: [[Models]] is how you run the project,
[[Modeling]] is how you describe the system.
